title: Persia
hookLine: Jews in Iran since Esther's day, a community that endures

lines: A STORY SET IN A PERSIAN PALACE.
cards: At Purim, Jews read aloud a story set in a Persian palace. A king named Ahasuerus. A queen named Esther who hides that she is Jewish.
Her cousin Mordecai at the palace gate. An enemy, Haman, with a plan. Heard from far away, the palace is just a setting.

But in the city of Hamadan stands a domed building where, tradition says, Esther and Mordecai are buried, and Persian Jews have visited it for generations. For them, the story is local. Today, Persia.

teach.b: Persia appears all through the later books of the Tanakh, not only in Esther. In Ezra, a Persian king, Cyrus, lets the exiles from Babylon go home and rebuild the Temple.
Isaiah goes further, and has God speak to a foreign king by name: "Thus saith the LORD to His anointed, to Cyrus." Daniel serves Persian kings.
Nehemiah is cupbearer in the palace at Shushan before he goes to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem.

teach.h: DANGER AND RESCUE IN ONE LAND.
teach.b: So Persia is the place of both danger and rescue. Haman's plot is hatched there. So is the decree that lets the people return.
And not everyone returned. Jewish families stayed in Persia, in Hamadan, Isfahan, Shiraz and other cities, through empire after empire.
They spoke Persian and wrote it in Hebrew letters, a language scholars call Judeo-Persian, and copied and translated the Bible in it.
Their life was sometimes peaceful and sometimes very hard, with times of forced conversion and times of quiet.
Persian Jewish families have also left, to Israel, to the United States, to other places, carrying Persian food, music and Purim customs with them.
And a Jewish community still lives in Iran today, with synagogues and schools. That is what the line since Esther means.
Not a story about long ago, but a people who stayed in the same land as the story, and are still there.

how: Persian Jewish families, in Iran and abroad, keep Persian foods and melodies at Shabbat and holiday tables, read the Esther scroll at Purim, and some visit the tomb in Hamadan that tradition links to Esther and Mordecai.

games.q: you are reading Isaiah, and God speaks to a foreign king by name, calling him His anointed. which king?
games.why: "Thus saith the LORD to His anointed, to Cyrus." the Persian king who, in Ezra, lets the exiles go home.

practice: Bring to mind the domed tomb in Hamadan, and the families who have visited it for generations. Then call to mind one place you love that has a long story behind it, and hold the people who stayed there through hard times.

wordCard.voice: Persia. The land of Esther and Cyrus, where Jews have lived, spoken Judeo-Persian and kept their faith through many empires, and where a community still lives today. Today's word.
